description: Hello we are planning to build a project related to challenge Be an Earth system trend detective
summary:
Kerala Trend Detective answers a simple question: is Kerala's climate really changing, and can we prove it? Earth science data has many variables and many regions, and a trend in one place can be the opposite in another, so it is hard to know what to look at. Our tool does that work and shows the answer in plain language.
We used NASA POWER monthly data (1991-2025). The tool covers five variables: rainfall, air temperature, root-zone soil wetness, surface soil wetness and relative humidity. For any variable, season and district, it calculates the yearly value, tests for a trend with the Mann-Kendall test, and measures the size of the change with Sen's slope. A trend is called significant when p < 0.05.
We ran 350 tests and built two things: a Google Colab notebook with an interactive selector, and a web dashboard with a district map, a trend chart with a plain-English verdict, and a comparison table for all districts.
What we found: air temperature is rising significantly in 13 of 14 districts on an annual basis (about 0.5 to 0.9 degrees C over 35 years), and in all 14 districts during the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons. Monsoon (June-September) rainfall shows no significant trend in any district. Pre-monsoon (March-May) rainfall is increasing significantly in 12 districts.
The result that monsoon rainfall is not significantly changing is as important as the warming result: it shows the tool separates real trends from natural year-to-year variation.
details:
What it does and how it works
Kerala Trend Detective shows what is changing in Kerala’s climate, where it is changing, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. The user picks a variable (rainfall, 2 m air temperature, root-zone soil wetness, surface soil wetness or relative humidity), a season (annual, monsoon, pre-monsoon, post-monsoon or winter) and a district. We download monthly NASA POWER data for 1991-2025 for all 14 districts and average each season into one value per year. We then run the Mann-Kendall trend test (significant if p < 0.05) and measure the size of the change with Sen’s slope. A Google Colab notebook runs all 350 tests (14 districts × 5 variables × 5 seasons). A web dashboard shows the results as a district map, a trend chart, a comparison table and a plain-English verdict.

What we found
Annual temperature is rising significantly in 13 of 14 districts, by about 0.5 to 0.9 °C over 35 years. Monsoon (June-September) rainfall shows no significant trend in any district. Pre-monsoon (March-May) rainfall is rising significantly in 12 districts.

Benefits and intended impact
The tool lets students, planners and farmers see real local trends without needing statistics knowledge. It separates real change from natural year-to-year variation, and it reports “no significant change” honestly instead of forcing a story. It can support seasonal planning for agriculture and water use, and it teaches what “statistically significant” means using local data.

Tools and technology
Python, Google Colab, requests, numpy, pandas, pymannkendall, matplotlib, ipywidgets, HTML and JavaScript (the dashboard), GitHub and GitHub Pages. We used the NASA POWER API, which needs no login, so anyone can re-run our work. No special hardware was needed. We built the code and dashboard with AI assistance from Claude and ChatGPT, as explained in our AI disclosure(ReadMe file in github).

Creativity
Instead of showing raw charts, the dashboard turns each test into a plain-English verdict. It treats “no proven trend” as a valid result, and its map and comparison table show whether the same variable behaves differently across districts. The notebook can be reused for any region or variable by changing the coordinates and parameter codes.

Factors we considered
We chose NASA POWER for open, reproducible access. We used seasons because Kerala’s climate depends strongly on the monsoon. We noted that the data grid is coarse (about 50 km), that running 350 tests means about 5% of “significant” results could be chance, and that 35 years is a short record. A significant trend shows change over time, not its cause. Re-running the notebook gave identical results.

Links
Live dashboard: https://faizanshiroj.github.io/kerala-trend-detective/
Code and data: https://github.com/faizanshiroj/kerala-trend-detective
